title: Google Docs and Gemini Notebook replaced my Obsidian vault for good
excerpt: Here's why I moved my notes from Obsidian
content_html:
Published Nov 16, 2026, 8:45 AM EST

I cover Android with a focus on productivity, automation, and Google’s ecosystem, including Gemini and everyday apps. With a background in engineering and software development, I tend to go beyond surface-level tips.
Before joining AP, I wrote for tech publications such as Gizbot in 2023 and iJunkie (formerly known as iPhoneHacks) from 2021 to 2022.

I used to rely on Obsidian to organize my notes, research, and ideas. It offered everything I wanted from a personal knowledge management tool, but maintaining a separate vault and keeping everything organized could sometimes feel tedious.

Then I discovered I could get much of what I wanted by combining Google Docs and Gemini Notebook.

Google Docs' Markdown support makes it easier to organize and work with my notes. Meanwhile, Gemini Notebook turns those documents into a searchable resource I can explore, summarize, and ask questions about.

Together, they've made managing my research simpler, and I haven't looked back at Obsidian.

Why I stopped relying on Obsidian

I wanted an easier way to organize my notes

Obsidian appealed to me because it offered a flexible way to organize my notes. I could create separate notes for different topics, connect related information using internal links, and use Markdown to keep everything neatly formatted.

However, I gradually realized I was spending too much time organizing my notes. Maintaining a vault, deciding where new information belonged, and keeping related ideas connected started feeling like extra work.

Using Obsidian was getting unnecessarily complicated. Its extensive plugin ecosystem is one of its biggest selling points, but choosing plugins, configuring them, and making sure everything works together can become a project of its own.

I also wanted an easier way to revisit my research and extract information. Having everything neatly organized is helpful, but finding connections across dozens of notes or getting answers from information I've collected is another challenge.

Google Docs has everything I need to organize my notes

Markdown makes it a better note-taking app

I use Google Docs to write articles and store longer documents, but I realized it could handle much of my everyday note-taking, too.

Markdown support in Google Docs is one of the main reasons I started considering it for note-taking. Instead of relying entirely on the formatting toolbar, I use Markdown syntax to structure my notes, format text, add headings, and create lists.

Here's how to enable Markdown in Google Docs:

  1. Open a document in Google Docs on your computer.
  2. Click Tools and select Preferences.
  3. Find and tick the Enable Markdown checkbox.
  4. Click OK to save your preference.

After it's enabled, you can use Markdown syntax while writing. For instance, typing ## Research notes creates a second-level heading, while wrapping text in double asterisks makes it bold.

One big advantage is that I don't have to think too much about organizing or maintaining a separate vault. I create individual documents for different topics and keep everything accessible through Google Drive.

I can take my notes anywhere with Markdown

My notes aren't locked into Google's ecosystem

One concern I had about moving away from Obsidian was whether I'd lose the flexibility of working with Markdown files.

After all, one of Obsidian's biggest advantages is that it stores notes as ordinary Markdown files, which I can open and edit in other apps. Fortunately, Google Docs offers similar flexibility. I can export any document as a Markdown file and take it to another app.

To do this, open a document in Google Docs, go to File > Download > Markdown (.md), and save the exported file. You can open it in Obsidian or any other Markdown-compatible editor.

If you want to move existing notes into Google Docs, you can also upload Markdown to Drive and open them with Google Docs.

Google has made Markdown support more useful by allowing users to open and edit .md files in Docs without converting them into Google Docs format.

This means I can work with Markdown files while using Docs' collaboration and editing features.

I don't have to choose between Google's convenience and Markdown's portability. I can keep my notes in Docs and Drive, use Gemini Notebook to explore them, and still take my files elsewhere if I decide to switch apps.

I organize my notes without building an Obsidian vault

Google Drive takes care of it

After moving away from Obsidian, I wanted to avoid recreating the same note-taking system in another app.

I create separate documents for different topics, projects, and research areas instead of putting everything into one document.

For longer notes, I use headings and subheadings to divide information into sections, making it easier to scan and find what I need. I also use bulleted and numbered lists, tables, and links to keep related information together.

Google Drive does much of the organizational work, too. I create folders for different projects, move relevant documents into them, and use descriptive file names, so I know what's inside without opening every document.

Since Docs saves changes automatically, I don't have to manually manage individual Markdown files or keep a separate vault in sync.

And when I need to do more with those notes, I bring them into Gemini Notebook.

Gemini Notebook makes my collection of notes more useful

It became a searchable library

Storing information is only half the problem. I also want to ask questions about what I've collected without opening dozens of documents.

Gemini Notebook supports several source formats, including Google Docs, PDFs, text files, and Markdown files. I can create a notebook for a particular project or subject and add the relevant research materials as sources.

For instance, I could create a notebook for a technology research project and add my Markdown notes, reference documents, and other relevant materials. Rather than manually browsing through all those files, I can ask Gemini Notebook questions about their contents.

I don't miss Obsidian anymore

If you rely on Obsidian's extensive plugin ecosystem, backlinks, graph view, local-first storage, or advanced customization, Google Docs and Gemini Notebook might feel limiting.

Obsidian is the better choice if you want complete control over how you build and manage a personal knowledge base.

But I'd rather spend my time writing and using my notes rather than organizing a vault, configuring plugins, and figuring out how to connect everything.

The best part is that I still get the flexibility of Markdown in Docs, the convenience of Google Drive, and Gemini Notebook's research capabilities.
